why.title: Why political donation transparency matters
why.p0: Democracy depends on informed citizens. By making political donation data accessible and easy to explore, we help people understand the financial relationships that shape their political landscape. Transparency in political financing builds trust, strengthens accountability, and empowers voters to make informed decisions.

what.title: What is this?
what.summary:
Party donations are an important part of politics. They are an important indicator of political support.

We try to present this data clearly and comprehensibly.
what.threshold: Due to the high number of minor political parties, we only track donations for parties that meet a specific threshold. The current threshold is set at {count} donations or a total of {sum} in contributions to that party, regardless of the size of individual donations.

source.austria:
The data used here comes from the Austrian Court of Audit and includes all party donations documented there since 2012.

Please note: Before July 8, 2019, political parties had to report individual donations of over 51,000 euros (until 2018 over 50,000 euros) to the ACA. Since July 2019, the reporting limit has been 2,500 euros.

The parties' data is normally updated on a quarterly basis.
source.germany: The data used here comes from the German Bundestag and includes all party donations over €50,000 documented there since 2010 and over €35,000 since March 5, 2024.
source.switzerland: The data used here comes from the Swiss Federal Finance Control and includes all political donations documented there since 2023.
source.netherlands:
The information presented here is sourced from the Government of the Netherlands and includes all political donations recorded since 2022 that exceed €1,000, as reported in the annual “Overzicht van giften aan politieke partijen en hun neveninstellingen”.

For the current year, only donations exceeding €10,000 are included, based on the “Overzicht substantiële giften aan politieke partijen” dataset.

Please note: Some donations lack specific date information and therefore are not included in time-series or other date-based visualizations.

Donations reported for SP and GL may appear relatively high because both parties require their MPs and administrators to contribute a substantial portion of their salaries to the party.
source.europeanunion:
The data presented here is sourced from the Authority for European Political Parties and European Political Foundations, encompassing all documented party and foundation donations since 2018. Due to the importance of European political foundations, we track and display their donations similarly to those of European political parties.

As the official data does not include data, no time series or similar visual representations are available.

Note that in the run-up to the 2024 European elections (from December 6, 2023 to June 10, 2024), special reporting requirements for donations applied, with weekly reports and timely publication by the authority.
Since June 10, 2024, only donations over 12,000 euros must be reported immediately. Other donations will only be available after the annual financial statements have been submitted.
source.estonia:
The data used here comes from the Estonian Party Funding Monitoring Committee and includes all political donations documented there since 2014 that exceed 1 euro.

Political parties in Estonia are required to report their income, including donations received, on a quarterly basis.
The data on the committee's website is updated accordingly on a quarterly basis.
source.czechrepublic:
The data used here comes from the Office for the Control of the Administration of Political Parties and Political Movements and includes all political donations documented there since 2018 that exceed CZK 25.

This scope also encompasses all contributions to parties or political movements that have either received more than 100 individual donations or surpassed 1 million CZK in total donation amounts, regardless of individual contribution sizes. The data is updated annually.
Donor type detection is based on identifying a donor as an Individual if both firstName and lastName fields are present.
source.latvia: The data used here comes from the Corruption Prevention and Combating Office and includes all political donations documented there since 2015, exceeding €1.
source.australia:
The data used here comes from the Australian Electoral Commission (AEC) and specifically from the "Donations Made Details" dataset that the AEC publishes. It includes all political donations documented there since 2014, exceeding €1.

It's worth noting that the AEC dataset may contain some typographical errors, which could result in certain donations being unaccounted for or not properly assigned to a specific party due to data entry inconsistencies. Additionally, the AEC's annual disclosures are released on February 1 each year, but the data does not provide a complete picture of all contributions due to the disclosure threshold of $15,000.

Donor types are classified by matching donor names. All common trade unions are manually mapped to the Trade Union donor type. Companies are detected by checking for specific corporate identifiers in the donor name: 'Pty' (Proprietary), 'Ltd' at the end of the name, 'Corporation', or 'Corp'.
source.unitedkingdom:
The data used here comes from the Electoral Commission and includes all political donations that have been documented there since 2010 and exceed £1,000.

The donation data is updated quarterly.
source.serbia:
The data used here does not come from the government, but from the non-profit organization “Center for Investigative Journalism of Serbia” (“Centar za istraživačko novinarstvo Srbije” - CINS), which has kindly aggregated the donation data of the Serbian Anti-Corruption Agency.

This data includes all political donations documented there since 2015.

As the dataset does not provide specific date information for individual donations, it is unfortunately not possible to display timelines or other time-based visualizations.
source.croatia:
The data used here comes from the State Electoral Commission of the Republic of Croatia (DIP) and includes all political donations with a monetary value exceeding €1, documented since 2019.
The dataset uses only the last donation document published for each reporting year (as reported by izbori) to avoid duplicates from earlier versions of the same year’s report.
All donations are displayed in Euro, while the underlying dataset uses Kuna until 2024. Donations originally made in Kuna are converted to Euro using approximate exchange rates for each half-year period from 2019 to 2024: H1 (0.1340, 0.1335, 0.1332, 0.1329, 0.1326) and H2 (0.1341, 0.1338, 0.1334, 0.1327, 0.1328).
source.canada: The data used here comes from Elections Canada and is based on the "contributions as submitted" dataset. It includes all political donations with a monetary value exceeding €500, documented since 2015. All entries that are part of the "Statement of Contributions Received" report from the "Annual" electoral event to "Registered parties" are included.
source.georgia: The information presented here is sourced from the Anti-Corruption Bureau (ანტიკორუფციული ბიურო﻿) of Georgia and includes all political donations recorded since 2011 that exceed 1 GEL. The dataset comprises only contributions classified as type #10 (Monetary donations) or type #16 (Monetary donations made by legal entities).
source.norway:
The data used here comes from the official party funding publications by Statistics Norway (SSB) and Partifinansiering.no. Totals shown are aggregated from multiple reported receiver entities (such as central, regional, local, and youth units) into a single total per party, with the underlying receiver mapping kept available for transparency.

The Norway dataset is refreshed on an annual update cycle, reflecting the cadence of the underlying disclosures.
source.ukraine:
The data used here is sourced from the National Agency on Corruption Prevention (NAZK) via the PolitData portal. It includes all records identified as "monetary contributions" in the official reports.

Note on Data Scope: This total reflects direct financial transfers only. It does not include state funding provided to parliamentary parties or in-kind (non-monetary) contributions such as goods and services.

Due to the full-scale Russian invasion, mandatory political party reporting was suspended from early 2022 until late 2023 for security and logistical reasons. Following the adoption of Law 3337-IX, parties are now backfilling their reports. Data for 2022–2025 is still being updated as the NAZK processes these submissions.

donor.ubo_description: An Ultimate Beneficial Owner (UBO) is the person who actually pulls the strings. They are the individuals who ultimately own or control the donor, typically by holding 25% or more of its shares or voting rights. If no single person meets this threshold, senior management (like Directors) may be listed as "pseudo-UBOs" to ensure accountability.

about.title: About

description.p0: DonationWatch emerged from frustration with the lack of easily readable data on the official site of the German Bundestag.
description.p1: Our aim is to enhance this by utilizing publicly available data and presenting it more effectively.
description.p2: We noticed that countries like Austria, Switzerland, and the Netherlands publish their political donations in various structured formats. To create a unified interface that simplifies access to this information, we have included these countries in our project. More countries will be added as we find and process the relevant data.

transparency.title: Transparency
transparency.p0: We strive to provide clear and consistent information about political party donors. To achieve this, we automatically normalize certain donor names to ensure uniformity across our database. This approach allows us to maintain accuracy while accounting for discrepancies in how names may be recorded.
transparency.p1: In the interest of transparency, we've compiled a list of normalized names along with their variations encountered in our donation records. Below, you'll find each normalized name followed by its variations. This list helps explain why you might see donor names that don't appear exactly in our source documents.

filtered_donors.p0: To accurately represent the true sources of political donations, we filter out certain transactions that are actually governmental contributions rather than genuine donations. Because our source datasets do not explicitly label these, we rely on a set of regular expression (regexp) filtering rules to automatically identify and remove such entries. You can review the full list of applied regexp filter rules below.
filtered_donors.p1: Below is a list of donors whose contributions were filtered out according to our criteria and filtering rules.

filtered_receivers.p0: To ensure we only present meaningful recipient data, we also filter out certain receivers or parties that are deemed irrelevant or non-operational for donor-tracking purposes. Since our datasets do not always label these receivers explicitly, we apply a set of regexp-based rules to automatically exclude them.
filtered_receivers.p1: You can review the full list of applied regexp filter rules below.

receivers.title: Aggregated Receivers
receivers.p0: In {country}, donations may be reported to different organizational units within a party. For consistency, we consolidates related receiver entities into one party-level total. The list below documents which receiver entities are aggregated into each party.
